Fargo by the numbers

Where is Fargo and how is the city laid out?

Fargo is the seat of Cass County, North Dakota, and it sits on the western bank of the Red River of the North in the flat Red River Valley. The city covers about 50.8 square miles at an elevation of roughly 906 feet.

Across the river is Moorhead, Minnesota, and the two cities together form the Fargo-Moorhead metro area. Interstates 29 and 94 cross in Fargo, and US 10, US 52 and US 81 also run through town. For a seller that matters in a plain way: a house on the Fargo side of the river is taxed under North Dakota rules, while a house in Moorhead falls under Minnesota law and a different county.

The valley floor is the bed of Glacial Lake Agassiz, which drained about 9,300 years ago and left the land very level.

What is the short history of Fargo?

Fargo was founded in 1871 and incorporated in 1874, and it was first called Centralia before being renamed for William Fargo, a Northern Pacific Railway director. The railroad drove early growth, and the town later became known as a gateway to the west.

On June 7, 1893, a fire destroyed 31 downtown blocks. More than 246 buildings went up within a year, in brick, with new streets and a water system. Homes near downtown can therefore be a century old or more.

The city has kept growing. Census counts run from 90,599 in 2000 to 105,549 in 2010 and 125,990 in 2020, with a 2024 estimate of 136,285.

Who are the largest employers around Fargo?

Health care, education and retail dominate Fargo employment. The city's annual financial report, as summarized on Wikipedia, lists these as its largest employers by full-time equivalent staff.

EmployerFull-time equivalents
Sanford Health6,278
Essentia Health2,848
West Fargo Public Schools2,541
North Dakota State University2,167
Fargo Public Schools2,064
VA Health Care System1,380
City of Fargo1,125

North Dakota State University, founded in 1890, and the Tri-College University partnership with Minnesota State University Moorhead and Concordia College bring a large student population. Fargo Public Schools runs 15 elementary schools, 3 middle schools and 4 high schools, and West Fargo Public Schools serves the southwestern part of the city.

What does Fargo weather mean for a house?

Fargo has a humid continental climate with long, hard winters, so heating costs, insulation and roof condition matter more here than in most of the country. January's normal mean is 9.2 degrees Fahrenheit, and the city sees about 43 days a year at or below zero.

Average snowfall is 51.4 inches and average precipitation is 24.0 inches. Summers are warm and humid, with a July mean of 70.7 degrees.

  • Roof and attic insulation, which buyers and inspectors check first
  • Furnace age and capacity
  • Basement moisture and sump pump function
  • Window and door seals

A cash buyer prices these items in directly, so you do not negotiate repair requests after an inspection.

How serious is Red River flooding in Fargo?

Flooding is the main natural hazard in Fargo. The Red River's minor flood stage here is 18 feet and major flooding begins at 30 feet.

YearRed River crest at Fargo
199739.5 feet
200940.84 feet (record)
201037 feet

As of 2012 the city had bought 700 houses in flood-prone areas, and residents sandbagged in 2009. The FM Area Diversion is the large permanent project meant to protect the metro area. The Metro Flood Diversion Authority says construction began in 2017 with a target of 2027, and its status page, updated in November 2026, shows the City of Fargo's portion at 90 percent while the Cass County portion shows 5 percent.

If your home sits in a flood-prone part of town, say so early. Buyers will ask about it, and the price will reflect it.

Who bills and collects property tax in Fargo?

The City of Fargo assessor values your home, and Cass County sends the bill and collects the money. The assessor appraises property as of February 1 each year and does not set the tax rate.

Rates come from the budgets of each taxing body. Elected city and county commissioners and school and park board members set what they need, and the mill levy is that amount divided by total taxable value. Cass County mails real estate statements in early December to the owner of record as of November 1, and a mortgage company also gets a copy.

The Cass County Finance Office takes payments at 211 9th Street South in Fargo, by mail, through a secure drop box, or online. The office phone is (701) 241-5600 for property tax questions.

When is Fargo property tax due and what are the penalties?

Real estate tax in Cass County can be paid in full by February 15 for a 5 percent discount, or in two installments due March 1 and October 15. Special assessments and drain taxes ride with the first installment and do not get the discount.

DateWhat happens
February 15Last day to pay in full and take the 5% discount
March 1First installment and specials due
After March 13% penalty on first installment
After May 16% total
After July 19% total
After October 1512% total on the first installment; 6% on the second installment

If a deadline lands on a weekend or county holiday, it moves to the next business day. Mailed payments count if postmarked by the deadline. Older delinquent real estate tax also earns interest of 1 percent per month on Cass County's schedule.

The penalty rules are in North Dakota Century Code section 57-20-01 and the discount is in section 57-20-09. Not receiving a statement does not extend the discount.

What are special assessments and drain taxes on a Fargo tax bill?

Special assessments are charges for infrastructure that benefits specific parcels, and drain taxes fund water or drainage projects for specific parcels. Both appear on the county statement, and neither qualifies for the 5 percent discount.

Cass County says a special assessment can be paid off at any time, and until then a yearly installment is billed. Some drain taxes are one-time balances and others are ongoing maintenance charges.

When you sell, ask the title company to list every remaining special and drain balance. Buyers and lenders will want the payoff or a clear plan for who carries it.

Which credits and exemptions might apply to a Fargo home?

Several state and city programs reduce a Fargo bill, and eligibility depends on the owner, not the buyer. The Cass County page lists the main ones.

  • Primary Residence Credit, up to $500 against 2024 taxes, applied for through the State Tax Commissioner
  • Homestead Credit for owners 65 or older or permanently and totally disabled
  • Disabled Veteran's Credit for a service-connected disability of 50 percent or more
  • Two-year new construction abatement that can reduce taxable true and full value by $150,000

The City of Fargo also offers a five-year exemption on value added by remodeling on buildings 25 years old or older. A renovation in an older Fargo house can therefore sit outside the tax base for a time, which is worth noting if you finished work before listing.

What if I disagree with my Fargo assessment?

Start with the Fargo assessor, then use the board of equalization steps, which run in a set order each year. State rules give local boards the first 15 days of April, county boards the first 10 days of June, and the State Board of Equalization the second Tuesday in August.

  • The state board can only reduce a value if you appealed to both the local and county boards
  • Each owner receives a written notice showing true and full value for the current and previous year
  • If the boards do not resolve it, you can apply for abatement by November 1 of the year after the tax becomes payable

Bring evidence such as comparable sales, an appraisal or repair estimates. The assessor values by mass appraisal, so condition problems the office cannot see are your best argument.

How does selling a Fargo house with tax due work?

You can sell a Fargo house with tax owing, and the unpaid amount is normally settled from the sale proceeds at closing. Cass County says current-year taxes must be paid in full before a deed can be recorded to transfer ownership.

The title company reads the county's figures, adds any special assessments, and pays the county from your proceeds. North Dakota does not charge a deed or mortgage tax, according to the Grand Forks County Recorder's page, so recording costs are fees rather than a transfer tax.

Cass County's delinquency calendar shows why waiting costs money. Statements of Taxes Owing go out in March, May, July and October, and Notices of Tax Lien go out in November. In May, certified Notices of Foreclosure of Tax Lien go to parcels with three years of unpaid taxes.

If the debt is old, a quick sale can protect your equity. Our team can review the county balance with you and make a written offer on the house as it stands, with no repairs and no commissions.

More questions about Fargo, ND Property Tax Guide

Who collects property tax in Fargo?

Cass County collects it. The City of Fargo Assessment Department sets the value, and the county Finance Office sends statements and takes payments at 211 9th Street South.

When is Fargo property tax due?

Real estate tax is due in two installments on March 1 and October 15, or in full by February 15 for a 5 percent discount. Penalties begin after March 1 on the first installment.

Can I sell my Fargo house if I owe back taxes?

Yes. Back taxes are paid from the proceeds at closing, and Cass County requires current-year taxes to be paid before a deed is recorded.

Does North Dakota have a deed transfer tax?

No. The Grand Forks County Recorder states that North Dakota has no deed or mortgage tax, though recording fees still apply.

What happens if Fargo property taxes stay unpaid for three years?

The county can start tax lien foreclosure. Cass County sends certified foreclosure notices each May for parcels with three years of unpaid taxes, and the owner can still pay up to October 1.

Bismarck by the numbers

Who sends a Bismarck property tax bill?

Burleigh County sends the bill, and the City of Bismarck sets the value. The city's Assessing Division values property inside city limits, and the Burleigh County Auditor/Treasurer mails the statement, collects the money and passes it to the taxing districts each month.

The county says that in Bismarck it controls less than 13 percent of the total bill. The rest goes to the city, the school district and other local districts, and the county has no authority over those levies. If a bill looks high, the right place to ask is the city assessor for the value or the district for its levy, not the treasurer.

The county's office is at 221 N 5th Street, Bismarck, ND 58501, phone 701-222-6718. The mailing address is PO Box 5518, Bismarck, ND 58506.

What should a seller know about Bismarck itself?

Bismarck is North Dakota's capital and the seat of Burleigh County, on the east bank of the Missouri River across from Mandan. It covers about 36.5 square miles and sits at 1,745 feet. It was incorporated on January 14, 1875, became capital of Dakota Territory in 1883 and the state capital in 1889. It is the only state capital named for a foreign statesman.

The 2020 census counted 73,622 residents, with an estimate of 77,772 for 2024. State government is the largest employer, followed by health care and schools. The 2024 city financial report lists these employers:

EmployerEmployees
State of North Dakota4,456
Sanford Health4,024
Bismarck Public Schools3,385
Bobcat/Doosan1,280
CHI St. Alexius Medical Center1,270

How does Bismarck's climate and river affect a house?

Bismarck has cold, snowy, windy winters and warm, humid summers. January averages 12.8 degrees Fahrenheit and July 71.3. Snowfall averages 50.5 inches a year and precipitation 19.05 inches, mostly from May to September.

For a house that means roofs carry a long snow season, heating systems matter, and a failed furnace in January becomes an emergency. The Garrison Dam, finished in 1953, improved flood control on the Missouri and made the south side more practical to develop, but the upper river still floods seasonally. If your home is near the river or a creek, check its flood map status before you sell.

Interstate 94 runs east and west through the city, US 83 joins it in north Bismarck, and Bismarck Municipal Airport south of town has the largest passenger volume in western North Dakota. Bismarck Public Schools runs 16 elementary schools, three middle schools, three public high schools and one alternative high school, and enrolled 13,976 students in 2023-2024.

How is a Bismarck property tax bill calculated?

North Dakota multiplies taxable value by the combined mill levy. Market value, called true and full value, is set by the assessor. Assessed value is 50 percent of that, and taxable value is 9 percent of assessed value for residential property and 10 percent for commercial and agricultural property.

The county's 2025 mill levy sheet lists a total of 237.10 mills for the City of Bismarck taxing district. Using the county's own method, a house with a market value of $300,000 has an assessed value of $150,000 and a taxable value of $13,500. At 237.10 mills the consolidated tax would be about $3,201 before any credits or state-paid relief. That is an illustration of the formula, not a quote, so check your statement.

StepRule
True and full valueMarket value set by the assessor
Assessed value50% of true and full value
Taxable value9% of assessed (residential), 10% (other)
Consolidated taxTaxable value times total mill levy

Special assessments for streets, sidewalks and water and sewer lines are billed on the same statement. They usually run several years and include principal on the borrowing, so a seller with a long balance should ask the title company how it will be handled.

When are Bismarck property taxes due, and what does paying late cost?

Real estate tax is due January 1 and is payable without penalty until March 1, with a 5 percent discount if the full bill, specials included, is paid by February 15. Statements are mailed in December, and state law requires mailing by December 26.

Burleigh County's penalty schedule for real estate is:

DatePenalty on first installment and specials
March 23%
May 16%
July 19%
October 1512%

The second installment, due October 15, takes a 6 percent penalty on October 16. You can pay online through the county's property search, by phone at 1-800-272-9829 with jurisdiction code 4434, or by mail to the Burleigh County Auditor. E-checks cost $3.98 under $10,000 and $19.92 at $10,000 or more. Cards cost 3.61 percent with a $1.52 minimum. For the 5 percent discount a postmark on or before the deadline counts, but the county does not guarantee mail delivery.

How do you challenge a Bismarck assessment?

Start with the city's Assessing Division, then use the boards of equalization. The city board must meet in the first 15 days of April, and the county board meets in June. The State Board meets the second Tuesday of August, and you must have appeared before the city and county boards to reach it.

A sample 2025 notice from the city shows the pattern: the city board met April 1, 2025, at 5:15 p.m., and the county board met June 2, 2025, at 3:00 p.m., both at 221 N 5th Street. The city must mail written notice within 15 days after a board raises a value. The assessing office can be reached at 701-355-1630.

If you miss the boards, you can file for abatement with the county auditor under N.D.C.C. 57-23-04. The deadline is November 1 of the year after the tax becomes delinquent. For example, a 2021 tax needs an application by November 1, 2023.

What happens if Bismarck property tax goes unpaid?

Property becomes subject to foreclosure of the tax lien if taxes, specials and penalties stay unpaid into the third year. The county then follows a set calendar:

  • Before June 1: notice of foreclosure goes to owners and occupants.
  • Before August 1: the delinquent list is published in the official county newspaper.
  • October 1: the tax lien foreclosure date; payment in full is due by 5 p.m.
  • Third Tuesday of November: the annual tax sale.

You can bring the account current any time before the sale starts. The county posts sale notices at least 15 days ahead and publishes them at least 10 days ahead. The pages we opened do not give Burleigh County's interest rate on delinquent taxes, so ask the treasurer for a payoff figure.

What credits and exemptions can Bismarck owners ask about?

The county's Tax Equalization office lists several programs. Check each against current rules before applying:

  • Homestead credit for owners 65 or older or permanently and totally disabled, with an income limit the county lists as under $70,000
  • Disabled veteran credit for an honorable discharge and a VA rating of 50 percent or more
  • Exemptions for wheelchair use, blindness and paraplegic disabled veterans
  • Farm residence exemption, which needs a statement of farm gross income

The county page we read showed an application deadline that had already passed, so call 701-222-6693 before you assume a program is open.

How does selling with tax due work in Bismarck?

The title company pays unpaid property tax and any special assessment balance from your sale proceeds at closing. You do not have to find the money first. You do need a payoff figure from the Burleigh County Auditor/Treasurer, which should include penalties up to the closing date. City specials are paid through the City of Bismarck Special Assessments Department.

A cash buyer purchases the house as-is, so liens for taxes are simply part of the closing statement. We cannot promise an offer amount before we see the property, and you owe nothing if you decline.

More questions about Bismarck, ND Property Tax Guide

Who do I pay property tax to in Bismarck, ND?

You pay Burleigh County. The county auditor/treasurer's office at 221 N 5th Street collects the tax, and the City of Bismarck's Assessing Division sets the value.

What is the Bismarck property tax discount?

A 5 percent discount applies to the consolidated tax if the whole bill, including specials, is paid by February 15.

When does a Bismarck tax bill become late?

The first installment is payable without penalty until March 1. A 3 percent penalty starts March 2 and rises to 12 percent on October 15. The second installment takes 6 percent after October 15.

Can I appeal my Bismarck assessment after the April meeting?

Yes, through abatement. File with the county auditor by November 1 of the year after the tax becomes delinquent, under N.D.C.C. 57-23-04.

Can I sell a Bismarck house that has unpaid taxes?

Yes. The unpaid tax and specials are paid from the proceeds at closing, so ask the county for a payoff figure before you sign.

Grand Forks by the numbers

Where is Grand Forks and what is the city known for?

Grand Forks is the seat of Grand Forks County, on the western bank of the Red River of the North, where the Red Lake River joins it. The name refers to that fork. The city covers about 29.3 square miles at an elevation of roughly 837 feet, 74 miles north of Fargo-Moorhead and 145 miles south of Winnipeg.

East Grand Forks, Minnesota, sits across the river, and the two cities form a metro area of 104,184 people in the 2020 census. A seller in Grand Forks deals with North Dakota rules and the Grand Forks County offices, while a seller across the river deals with Minnesota.

The city has no lakes within its limits. The Red River and English Coulee cross it, and the old floodplain is now the Greater Grand Forks Greenway.

How did Grand Forks get started?

Grand Forks began as a fur-trading site that French traders called Les Grandes Fourches, and a U.S. post office opened there on June 15, 1870. Steamboat captain Alexander Griggs platted the town in 1875, and it was incorporated on February 22, 1881.

The University of North Dakota was established in 1883, six years before statehood. The Great Northern Railway arrived in 1880 and the Northern Pacific in 1887. In 1954 the city was chosen as the site of an Air Force base.

Population reached 59,166 in the 2020 census, up 12.0 percent from 52,838 in 2010. The median age is 30.2, which fits a university and military town.

Who employs people in Grand Forks?

The University of North Dakota is the largest employer in the metro area, and Altru Health System is the largest private employer. The city's 2024 annual financial report, as summarized on Wikipedia, gives these counts.

EmployerEmployees
University of North Dakota5,562
Altru Health System3,400
Grand Forks Air Force Base2,897
Grand Forks Public Schools1,700

The economy also includes manufacturing and food processing, and the state-owned North Dakota Mill and Elevator is described as the nation's largest flour mill.

Which schools and roads serve Grand Forks?

Grand Forks Public Schools enrolls about 7,400 students and runs ten elementary schools, the Twining combined school, three middle schools (Schroeder, South and Valley), and two high schools, Central and Red River. A nine-member elected board governs the district.

US 2, Interstate 29 and US 81 serve the city. Grand Forks International Airport has Delta service to Minneapolis-St. Paul and Allegiant flights to Mesa, Sanford and Las Vegas. Amtrak's Empire Builder stops daily, and Cities Area Transit, running since 1926, operates 12 bus routes.

  • I-29 and US 81 serve the city, and US 2 crosses it
  • Delta runs daily round trips to Minneapolis-St. Paul
  • Amtrak's Empire Builder stops daily

What does a Grand Forks winter and spring mean for a house?

Grand Forks has a warm-summer humid continental climate, with January daily highs averaging 15.8 degrees Fahrenheit and July highs averaging 80.7 degrees. The record low is minus 43 degrees from January 1912.

Average precipitation is 21.74 inches a year and average snowfall is 48.4 inches. A tight envelope, a sound roof and a working furnace carry more weight in a Grand Forks inspection than they would in a milder place.

Spring is the other season to plan around. Melting snow feeds the Red River, which leads to the story every Grand Forks homeowner knows.

How did the 1997 flood change Grand Forks housing?

The 1997 Red River flood did more damage in Grand Forks than in any other major valley city that year, and a downtown fire destroyed 11 buildings at the flood's peak. The peak flow was about 135,000 cubic feet per second, according to the city.

Flood protection factCity figure
Voluntary buyouts (1997-1998)850 properties
Dwellings demolished694
Houses moved161
English Coulee diversion channel9.5 miles
New pump stations12
Project cost, Grand Forks and East Grand Forks$409 million

Levee tops are about 10 feet wide, and floodwalls add 3 feet. The city says the system could handle a 500-year flood by adding clay to the levees. About 20 miles of greenway trails and a golf course now occupy the former floodplain.

For sellers, flood history is part of the conversation with any buyer, so know where your lot sits relative to the levee system.

Who values and who bills property tax in Grand Forks?

The City of Grand Forks Assessing Department values property inside the city, and the Grand Forks County Treasurer bills and collects the tax. City Assessor Tami Lazur leads the department, which also appraises new construction each year and checks exemption and credit claims.

The city inspects on a six-year cycle, reaching about one-sixth of properties each year. In an August 2025 Grand Forks Herald report, the assessor said owners may decline interior inspections, in which case the office judges from the outside. She summed that up as judging the whole book by its cover.

The assessing office is at City Hall, 255 N 4th Street. Email is GFAssessing@grandforksgov.com.

What are the Grand Forks property tax dates and penalties?

Statements are mailed by December 26. Taxes are due January 1 and can be paid without penalty until March 1, and a 5 percent discount applies to full payment by February 15.

DateRule under N.D.C.C. 57-20-01
February 155% discount if the full year is paid
March 1First installment due; 3% penalty after
May 1Additional 3%
July 1Additional 3%
October 15Second installment due; first-installment penalty grows by 3%; second installment carries 6% after

The county treasurer's mailing address is PO Box 5638, Grand Forks ND 58206-5638, and the phone is 701-780-8292. Online lookups run through the county's Tyler iTax and Vanguard property search pages.

What are special assessments in Grand Forks?

Special assessments are charges that split the cost of an infrastructure project among the properties that benefit, and the city says they are not property taxes. They can fund sidewalks, street paving and lighting, water main, storm sewer, sanitary sewer and flood protection.

Project typeRepayment term
Water mains, sanitary sewer, storm sewer25 years
Paving (asphalt or concrete)25 years
Street lighting, sidewalks, flood control20 years
Gravel or maintenance streets5 to 10 years

Questions go to the city Finance and Administrative Services Department, 255 N 4th Street, at 701-746-2671. Ask for the remaining balance before listing, since buyers and lenders will want the payoff figure. Flood control is one of the project types the city lists.

How do I appeal a Grand Forks assessment?

Appeal first to the city, which must hold a Board of Equalization meeting under state law, and written, phone or electronic appeals count as appearing in person. Written appeals go to tlazur@grandforksgov.com or PO Box 5200, Grand Forks ND 58206.

  • City board: first 15 days of April
  • County board: first 10 days of June
  • State board: second Tuesday in August, only if you appeared at the city and county boards
  • Abatement: by November 1 of the year after the tax becomes payable

Gather comparable sales, an appraisal or repair bids before the April meeting.

How does selling a Grand Forks house with tax owing work?

Unpaid property tax does not block a sale, because the title company pays the county from your proceeds at closing. Ask for a payoff figure that includes any special assessments and penalties.

Deeds are recorded at the Grand Forks County Recorder's Office, 151 South 4th Street, phone 701-780-8262. The Recorder's page states that North Dakota has no deed or mortgage tax, and it accepts electronic recording through Simplifile, CSC Recording Solutions, Indecomm and ePN.

State law lets a county foreclose a tax lien after taxes go unpaid into the third year, and an owner can stop it by paying everything owed by October 1. The county website posts a Notice of Foreclosure of Tax Lien each year. If you are behind, selling to a cash buyer before the notice arrives keeps options open. We buy Grand Forks houses as they are, and the title company handles the county payoff.

More questions about Grand Forks, ND Property Tax Guide

Who collects property tax in Grand Forks?

The Grand Forks County Treasurer. The City Assessing Department only values the property.

When is Grand Forks property tax due?

Tax is due January 1 and payable without penalty until March 1, with a 5 percent discount for full payment by February 15.

Can I sell a Grand Forks house with unpaid taxes?

Yes. The title company pays the owed taxes and special assessments from your closing proceeds.

How big was the 1997 flood buyout in Grand Forks?

The city bought 850 properties in its voluntary buyout program in 1997 and 1998, and about 694 dwellings were demolished.

Does North Dakota charge a deed tax when a house sells?

No. The Grand Forks County Recorder states that North Dakota has no deed or mortgage tax.
